messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Margaret's Story

Margaret was sixty-one when the chemical spill happened, a woman who had spent thirty years building a reputation as a meticulous policy analyst at the Department of Environmental Health. She had always prided herself on her competence, her ability to read a room, to anticipate problems before they materialized. On the afternoon of March 14th, she was reviewing air quality compliance reports in her office on the third floor of the state building when the alarm sounded—not the fire alarm, but something sharper, more urgent. Within minutes, the hallway filled with acrid smoke. A tanker truck carrying industrial solvents had overturned on the street below, and the fumes were rising through the ventilation system. Margaret remembered the smell most vividly: a caustic, chemical burn that coated her throat and made her eyes stream. She had walked out calmly, she thought, but her hands had shaken as she descended the stairwell. In the weeks after, she developed a persistent cough. The doctors said her lungs would recover, but something else didn't.

The smell of smoke—any smoke, whether from a barbecue or a distant wildfire—now triggered a cascade of physical reactions that Margaret couldn't control. Her heart would race, her breathing would tighten, and she would feel a deep, animal certainty that danger was imminent. The burnt smell of toast in her own kitchen made her stomach clench. Even the faint smell of alcohol on someone's breath—a sensory detail she couldn't quite explain to herself—would send her into a state of high alert, as though her nervous system had learned to recognize threat in scents that bore no logical connection to the spill. These triggers didn't simply remind her of what had happened; they seemed to confirm something she had come to believe about herself and the world: that she could not be trusted to recognize danger in time, that her judgment had failed her on that March afternoon and would fail her again. If she hadn't noticed the alarm quickly enough, if she had lingered in her office for even another minute, the exposure could have been worse. She was certain now that she couldn't rely on herself to keep herself safe.

This conviction—that she was fundamentally unreliable, that she couldn't trust her own instincts—began to reshape how Margaret moved through the world. She started scanning every room she entered before she sat down, mapping exits as a matter of compulsion. In the office, she repositioned her desk so she could see the door. At restaurants, she would ask to be seated where she could observe the entrance and watch the kitchen. Her colleagues noticed her tension but attributed it to stress. What they didn't see was the constant vigilance, the way Margaret's eyes moved to the windows whenever a siren passed, the way she would leave a room if someone lit a candle nearby. She had come to believe that her vigilance was the only thing standing between her and catastrophe—that if she stopped watching, stopped checking, something terrible would happen. And yet the watching itself was exhausting, and it only deepened her sense that she couldn't trust herself. If she was always on the verge of missing something critical, how could she ever feel secure?

Margaret's mind had begun to work against her in other ways too. She would lie awake at night, replaying the afternoon of the spill, imagining all the ways it could have been prevented. If she had left the office five minutes earlier. If she had suggested that morning that the building's ventilation system be inspected. If she had been more alert, more competent, more aware. This rumination consumed hours, and it only reinforced her sense of self-doubt—the conviction that she couldn't trust herself to do the right thing, that her judgment was fundamentally flawed. She began avoiding anything that might remind her of the event: she stopped watching the evening news, deleted news alerts from her phone, and asked her husband not to discuss current events in her presence. These strategies gave her temporary relief, but they also meant that she was increasingly withdrawing from the world, and with each withdrawal came another piece of evidence that she was broken, that the normal emotions and engagement she once felt were slipping away. She would never feel normal again, she was certain of it. The woman she had been before March 14th was gone.

Now, six months later, Margaret sits in the waiting room of a trauma specialist, her purse held tightly in her lap, her eyes moving toward the door every few seconds. Her husband has insisted she come. She has taken leave from work, telling her supervisor it was for personal reasons, though the real reason is that she can no longer trust herself to manage the unpredictability of the office. What Margaret fears most is that this feeling—this sense of being unsafe in her own skin, unable to rely on her own mind—will never lift. But there is also, beneath the fear, a small thread of hope that perhaps someone might help her understand why her mind and body have turned against her, and whether it's possible to feel like herself again.
